formula: a_point ~ I(gcse_tot / gcse_no - 6) + I((gcse_tot / gcse_no - 6)^2) + gender + (1 + I(gcse_tot / gcse_no - 6) | lea:estab)
notes: Read the help page example: runMLwiN(logit(a_point, cons, 6) ~ 1 + gcseav[1:5] + I(gcseav^2)[1:5] + gender[1:5] + (1[1:5] + gcseav[1:5] | school), D = 'Ordered Multinomial', EstM = 1) with gcseav = gcse_tot/gcse_no - 6 and school the lea and estab combination (the page: establishment codes alone do not identify schools). [1:5] gives one coefficient across the five cumulative logits, a proportional-odds model, so the family is the rule's cumulative logit; MCMC with MLwiN's default priors. pupil is the pupil id and cons the constant. RULE GAP: the random slope is on gcseav, a ratio of two columns; filed as gcse_tot|lea:estab, the formula carries the ratio.

Read the help page example: after relevel(use4, 4), runMLwiN(log(use4, cons) ~ 1 + lc + (1 | district), D = 'Unordered Multinomial', EstM = 1, nonlinear = c(1, 2)), Not_using_contraception the reference category. RULE GAP: an unordered multinomial logit (brms categorical) is outside Family, so family is blank. use is the binary recoding of use4 (alternate response), woman the level-1 id and cons the constant. lc is an ordered factor (the page: ordered levels; the example notes ordered predictors are fitted with treatment contrasts). 2867 women in 61 districts, a larger subset of the 1989 Bangladesh Fertility Survey than bang1.

formula: use ~ age + lc + urban + (1 + urban | district)
notes: Read the help page example: runMLwiN(logit(use, denomb) ~ 1 + age + lc + urban + (1 + urban | district), D = 'Binomial', EstM = 1) with denomb = 1, a Bernoulli logit with a correlated random intercept and urban slope by district (Browne 2012). woman is the id and cons the constant; lc is an ordered factor per the page. The 1934 women in 60 districts of mlmRev Contraception.

formula: votecons ~ defence + unemp + taxes + privat + (1 | area)
notes: Read the help page example: runMLwiN(logit(votecons, cons) ~ 1 + defence + unemp + taxes + privat + (1 | area), D = 'Binomial', EstM = 1); 800 voters in 110 constituencies of the 1983 British Election Study. voter is the id; cons and denom are constant columns of ones, cons the binomial denominator.

formula: cvddef ~ I(age^3) + I(age^3):I(log(age)) + sex + sex:I(age^3) + sex:I(age^3):I(log(age)) + (1 | area)
notes: Read the help page example from Leyland and Groenewegen (2020): runMLwiN(logit(cvddef) ~ 1 + I(age^3) + I(age^3):I(log(age)) + sex + sex:I(age^3) + sex:I(age^3):I(log(age)) + (1 | area), D = 'Binomial'), fitted by MQL1 and then PQL2. The fractional-polynomial age terms name age once, and sex:age stands for their interactions with sex. area is the postcode sector and id the respondent id; sc, carstair and smoke are not in the model. 1998 Scottish Health Survey, 8804 respondents.

Read the help page example: runMLwiN(n_ilea ~ 1 + n_vrq + (1 + n_vrq | school) + (1 | pupil)), IGLS with standardized residuals, leverage and influence stored. (1 | pupil) is MLwiN's level-1 residual, so the lme4 form has no pupil term and pupil, the level-1 id, is ignored. ilea and vrq are the raw scores whose normal scores are n_ilea and n_vrq. 907 pupils in 18 schools (Aitkin and Longford 1986).

formula: referral ~ pagegrp + patsex + diag + patedu + patinsur + gpexper + gpworkload + practype + location + gpphysifr + (1 | gpid)
notes: Read the help page example from Leyland and Groenewegen (2020): runMLwiN(logit(referral) ~ 1 + pagegrp + patsex + diag + patedu + patinsur + gpexper + gpworkload + practype + location + gpphysifr + (1 | gpid), D = 'Binomial'), MQL1 then PQL2, the ordered factors fitted with treatment contrasts. patid is the patient id; patage is the raw age that pagegrp groups (alternate coding). pagegrp and patedu are ordered factors per the page. 16700 patients of 100 Dutch general practices (1987).

Read the help page example: runMLwiN(c(written, csework) ~ 1 + female + (1 | school) + (1 | student), D = 'Multivariate Normal', EstM = 1), a bivariate model with correlated school effects and correlated student-level residuals; one row per response in the page's order. (1 | student) is the level of the residual covariance across the two responses, so student, the pupil id, is ignored. agemths is not in the model. 1905 pupils in 73 schools; mlmRev Gcsemv holds the same data.
Second response of the bivariate model in row 1 (the same runMLwiN call); written is the other response.

Read the help page example: runMLwiN(c(es_core, biol_core, biol_r3, biol_r4, phys_core, phys_r2) ~ 1 + female + (1 | school) + (1 | student), D = 'Multivariate Normal', EstM = 1), six correlated test scores of 2439 students in 99 schools (the page's description says women across districts, its format students in schools; Goldstein 2003). One row per response in the page's order, capped at three; biol_r4, phys_core and phys_r2 are the further responses, ignored in each row. (1 | student) holds the residual covariance across responses, so student is ignored.
Second response of the multivariate model in row 1 (the same runMLwiN call).
Third response of the multivariate model in row 1 (the same runMLwiN call); an optional biology test, missing for students who did not take it.

Read the help page example: runMLwiN(c(english, probit(behaviour, denomb)) ~ 1 + sex + ravens + fluent[1] + (1 | school) + (1[1] | id), D = c('Mixed', 'Normal', 'Binomial'), EstM = 1) with denomb = cons, a bivariate model of a Normal and a probit response with correlated school effects (Browne 2012). fluent[1] enters the english equation only; (1[1] | id) is the Normal response's level-1 variance, so id, the pupil id, is ignored. english is an integer score out of 100 fitted as Normal, so count with family gaussian. 1119 pupils in 47 schools of the Junior School Project.

Second response of the mixed-response model in row 1: probit(behaviour, denomb) with denomb = cons, a Bernoulli probit; fluent is not in its equation. behaviour is the bottom-quarter behavior rating against the rest (the page: three categories merged into two).

Read the help page example from Leyland and Groenewegen (2020, ch. 11): runMLwiN(smr ~ 1 + I(year - 79) + (1 | district) + (1 | ID)) with ID the row number, MLwiN's level-1 residual, so the lme4 form has no ID term. smr is deaths over expected times 100, so deaths and expected are ignored as its components. county and region are higher levels the example does not fit; family is the district classification, not in the model. 5639 district-years of 403 districts in England and Wales.

Read the help page example: runMLwiN(log(obs) ~ 1 + uvbi + offset(log(exp)) + (1 | nation) + (1 | region), D = 'Poisson', EstM = 1); 354 counties in 79 regions of 9 nations (Langford et al. 1998). county is the level-1 unit, exp the offset's column and cons the constant. mlmRev Mmmec holds the same data.

Read the help page examples: the variance components model normexam ~ 1 + (1 | school) + (1 | student) by IGLS and MCMC, the random-slope model runMLwiN(normexam ~ 1 + standlrt + (1 + standlrt | school) + (1 | student), EstM = 1), and the same with complex level-1 variance (1 + standlrt | student), all with one grouping, so one row, the random-slope model. (1 | student) is MLwiN's level-1 residual and student the pupil id. 4059 pupils in 65 schools; mlmRev Exam holds the same data.

Read the help page example: runMLwiN(attain ~ 1 + (1 | sid) + (1 | pid) + (1 | pupil), estoptions = list(xc = TRUE, EstM = 1)), secondary and primary schools cross-classified (Paterson 1991). (1 | pupil) is MLwiN's level-1 residual and pupil the id. attain is an integer attainment score from 1 to 10 fitted as Normal, so count with family gaussian, as mlmRev ScotsSec model 3. mlmRev ScotsSec holds the same 3435 Fife pupils.

Read the help page example: the same call as xc, runMLwiN(attain ~ 1 + (1 | sid) + (1 | pid) + (1 | pupil), estoptions = list(xc = TRUE, EstM = 1)), cited to Browne (2012). (1 | pupil) is MLwiN's level-1 residual. attain is filed count with family gaussian as in xc. RULE GAP: the page describes the same 3435 Fife pupils and columns as xc, here sorted by secondary school and stored as integers; filed as its own table for the merge's duplicate check.

formula: cbind(NumYes, NumNo) ~ factor(ContCntr) + I(1000 * TargCntr) + (0 + I(1000 * TargCntr) | Obs) + (1 + I(1000 * TargCntr) | Obs:ContCntr)
notes: Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch9.R (Knoblauch and Maloney 2012, ch. 9, mixed-effects models): with TrgCnt1000 = 1000 * TargCntr and FCtxCnt = factor(ContCntr), Context.glmm1 to Context.glmm3b compare random structures by anova and the final Context.glmm4 <- glmer(cbind(NumYes, NumNo) ~ FCtxCnt + TrgCnt1000 + (TrgCnt1000 + 0 | Obs) + (TrgCnt1000 | Obs:FCtxCnt), family = binomial('probit')). Six observers, four flanker contrasts, five target contrasts. RULE GAP: successes beside failures without a trials column are filed count (as faraway soybean), NumNo ignored; a binomial probit is outside Family, so family is blank; the by-observer term is a slope without an intercept, filed as TargCntr||Obs.

The help page names no model, only a lattice plot of Response against Contrast per Cell, and MPDiR's chapter scripts do not use the table. Six cells of macaque V1 and V2 at seven contrasts (Peirce 2007, on saturating contrast-response functions); Response is a mean firing rate over N trials with its SEM, an aggregate response on a real grouping, so low. Type and Area are cell-level columns. The linear form stands in for a contrast-response function.

Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch9.R (Knoblauch and Maloney 2012, ch. 9): clmm(factor(SimRating) ~ sibs + (1 | Obs), data = Faces, link = 'probit'), a cumulative probit with observer intercepts; chapter 3 fits the fixed clm and tests agediff and gendiff by addterm. Image (30 image pairs) is crossed with Obs (32 observers) and enters model 2. RULE GAP: SimRating is an 11-point rating (0 to 10), past the ordinal cap of ten levels, so it is filed count with family cumulative(probit).

formula: SimRating ~ sibs + (0 + sibs | Obs) + (0 + sibs | Image)
notes: Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch9.R: Faces.glmm <- polmer(SimRating ~ sibs + (sibs1 - 1 | Obs) + (sibs1 - 1 | Image), data = Faces, lnk = 'probit'); polmer, defined at the top of the script, expands the ratings into cumulative binary responses and fits glmer with a binomial probit, sibs1 the sibling indicator. RULE GAP: the random terms are slopes on sibs without intercepts, filed as sibs||Obs and sibs||Image; the 11-point response is filed count as in row 1.

Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch9.R: F2.glmm1 <- glmer(Resp ~ Stim + (1 | Obs) + (1 | Image), data = Faces2, family = binomial(probit)), crossed observers and image pairs read as a signal-detection model (d-prime and criterion); F2.glmm2 to F2.glmm4 add Stim slopes by Obs, Image or both and are compared by anova, the same grouping. RULE GAP: the first eight rows' Resp equal SimRating > 5 of the same observer and image pairs in Faces, so Faces2 may be Faces dichotomized; the page calls it a Yes/No judgment, and it is filed as its own table.

formula: cbind(round(N * p / 100), N - round(N * p / 100)) ~ log(Q) + (1 + log(Q) | Obs:Run)
notes: Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch1.R: after renaming Q and p to Quanta and PerCent, NumYes = round(N * PerCent/100) and id = interaction(Obs, Run), HSP1.glm <- glm(cbind(NumYes, NumNo) ~ id/log(Quanta) - 1, binomial(probit)) fits one probit psychometric function per observer and run, against HSP0.glm with one common function. The five functions (three observers, one of them with two runs; Hecht, Shlaer and Pirenne 1942) are rendered with random intercepts and log-quanta slopes at low, as a fixed-effects fit over blocks. p is a percentage, continuous with its denominator N in the formula. RULE GAP: a binomial probit is outside Family, so family is blank.

Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch2.R (Knoblauch and Maloney 2012, ch. 2): on the Gabor stimuli Stim1 to Stim10 (mfGab, a subset), mfGab.lmer <- lmer(LContSens ~ Stim + (1 | Obs)) and mfGab.lmer2 adding (1 | Obs:Stim), preferred by anova and refitted as lme(LContSens ~ Stim, random = ~ 1 | Obs/Stim); aov(LContSens ~ Stim + Error(Obs/Stim)) gives the same strata. 16 observers, 43 stimuli, four repeats each; the subset fit stays on the whole table.

Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch2.R: lm(LnThresh ~ Mtype + Sex + LnAge), interactions tested by update(. ~ .^2) and Sex dropped (Motion.lm2), a pooled fit. 70 observers, some with both a first- and a second-order threshold (112 rows; Thibault et al. 2007), so Subject is a grouping factor the source does not fit, rendered as a random intercept at medium.

formula: log_rt ~ task * stimulus * density * frequency + (1 + stimulus + frequency || id) + (1 + task | item)
notes: Read the afex vignette afex_mixed_example (Freeman, Heathcote, Chalmers and Hockley 2010): on the correct trials (fhch2010[fhch2010$correct, ], a subset) the maximal m1s, mixed(log_rt ~ task*stimulus*density*frequency + (stimulus*density*frequency|id) + (task|item)), is reduced through singular fits to the final m9s <- mixed(log_rt ~ task*stimulus*density*frequency + (stimulus+frequency||id) + (task|item), expand_re = TRUE). The help page example fits aov_ez('id', 'log_rt', between = 'task', within = c('density', 'frequency', 'length', 'stimulus')). rt is the untransformed response and correct marks the trials kept; length is not in the final model. 45 participants, 600 items.

formula: response ~ condition * believability * validity + (1 | id) + (1 | id:believability) + (1 | id:validity) + (1 | id:believability:validity)
notes: Read the help page example (Klauer and Singmann 2013, p. 1270): aov_ez('id', 'response', ks2013.3, between = 'condition', within = c('believability', 'validity')), a repeated-measures ANOVA on cell means, and the same per condition; translated to lme4 as one intercept per error stratum, the id:believability:validity stratum kept since each of the 60 participants gives four responses per cell (different contents). response is a liking rating fitted as Normal, so ordinal with family gaussian. content, the syllogism's content, is not in the model.

Read the help page examples (Maxwell and Delaney 2004, ch. 15): aov_4(iq ~ timecat + (timecat|id)), mixed(iq ~ timecat + (1|id)) (Table 15.3), mixed(iq ~ timecat + (1+time|id)) (Table 15.4) and the growth curve model mixed(iq ~ time + (1+time|id)) (Table 15.6), all grouped by child; filed the growth curve model, whose slope covariate is in its fixed part. timecat is time as a factor (alternate coding). 12 children at four ages. RULE GAP: the page calls the data hypothetical; kept as the registry's carData OBrienKaiserLong, contrived data, was.

Read the help page examples (Maxwell and Delaney 2004, Table 16.3): mixed(severity ~ sex + (1|id)), with treatment contrasts and with afex's sum contrasts; six clinical trainees (id), three per sex, each rating four clients. severity is an integer rating fitted as Normal, so count with family gaussian. RULE GAP: the page's description, copied from md_12.1, calls the data hypothetical; kept as the registry's carData OBrienKaiserLong, contrived data, was.

Read the help page example (Maxwell and Delaney 2004, Table 16.6): mixed(induct ~ cond + (1|room:cond)), six classrooms nested in condition (room numbered 1 to 3 within cond). obs is the child id; cog and skill are not in the model. induct is an integer reasoning score fitted as Normal, so count with family gaussian. RULE GAP: the page calls the study hypothetical; kept as the registry's carData OBrienKaiserLong, contrived data, was.

formula: value ~ treatment * gender * phase * hour + (1 | id) + (1 | id:phase) + (1 | id:hour)
notes: Read the afex aov_car help examples: aov_car(value ~ treatment * gender + Error(id/(phase*hour)), data = obk.long, observed = 'gender'), the mixed ANOVA on the full design (aov_car adds the within factors to the fixed part), translated to one intercept per error stratum; with one value per id, phase and hour, the id:phase:hour stratum is the residual. age is a covariate the page draws at random (sample(18:35)) for illustration, so ignored. RULE GAP: the page calls the data contrived, from an imaginary study (O'Brien and Kaiser 1985); kept as the registry's carData OBrienKaiserLong (hand-checked), whose long form this is with age added.

Read the afex mixed help examples: mixed(value ~ treatment * phase + (1|id), obk.long) and mixed(value ~ treatment*phase*hour + (1|id), per_parameter = '^hour$', method = 'nested-KR') with hour made an ordered factor; filed the larger model, subject intercepts only. age ignored and the contrived-data caveat as in row 1.

formula: response ~ instruction * inference * plausibility + (1 | id) + (1 | id:inference) + (1 | id:plausibility) + (1 | id:inference:plausibility)
notes: Read the afex vignette afex_anova_example: aov_ez('id', 'response', sk2011.1, between = 'instruction', within = c('inference', 'plausibility')), equivalent to aov_car(response ~ instruction + Error(id/inference*plausibility)); translated to one intercept per error stratum, id:inference:plausibility kept since each participant gives two responses per cell (different contents). The help page's examples (Singmann and Klauer 2011, Table 1) fit the same ANOVA with type for plausibility on the affirmation and denial problems separately. validity and what recode inference (alternate codings); type and content are not in this model. response is an integer rating from 0 to 100 fitted as Normal, so count with family gaussian.

formula: response ~ instruction * inference * type + (1 + inference * type | id)
notes: Read the afex mixed help examples: on the affirmation problems (sk2011.2[sk2011.2$what == 'affirmation', ], a subset) sk_m1 <- mixed(response ~ instruction*inference*type + (inference*type|id)), the maximal by-participant slopes, with an uncorrelated variant (inference*type||id) and an all_fit LRT variant; the inference:type slope stays in the formula only. The help page's examples fit aov_ez repeated-measures ANOVAs per problem kind after excluding eight participants (Singmann and Klauer 2011, Table 2). validity and what recode inference; content is not in the model. response is a 0 to 100 rating fitted as Normal, so count with family gaussian.

formula: acc ~ congruency * condition + (1 + congruency * condition | pno)
notes: Read the afex vignette afex_analysing_accuracy_data: on Experiment 1 (study == 1, acc not missing, a subset) e1_mixed1_v1 <- mixed(acc ~ congruency*condition + (congruency*condition|pno), family = binomial, method = 'LRT'), the maximal by-participant structure kept since no fit is singular; the vignette also fits it on cell proportions weighted by trials, and with study added on Experiments 1 and 2 (acc ~ congruency*condition*study + (congruency*condition|pno)). The congruency:condition slope stays in the formula only. rt is the other response; pno carries the study prefix, so participants nest in study. Lin et al. (2020), 685 participants in four studies.

formula: log(rt) ~ condition * congruency + (1 | pno) + (1 | pno:condition) + (1 | pno:congruency) + (1 | pno:condition:congruency)
notes: Read the afex vignette assumptions_of_ANOVAs: on Experiment 1 without missing values (a subset), aov_ez('pno', 'rt', stroop1, within = c('condition', 'congruency')) and, after its residuals fail the normality check, the same with transformation = 'log'; translated to one intercept per error stratum, the pno:condition:congruency stratum kept since the ANOVA averages many trials per cell. acc is the other response.

The page describes the design and fits no model: both soleus muscles of seven rats, one randomized to pinacidil and one to placebo, contraction force measured every 30 seconds on 15 occasions (Kristensen and Hansen 2004, a tutorial on repeated measures). Rendered with rat and muscle (rat:cond) intercepts and time as a factor. values are normalized to the first time point, so time 0 is 100 for every muscle.

The page describes a split-plot design and fits no model: six pregnant mice randomized to valproic acid or saline (group, constant within litter), their 24 offspring randomized to MPEP or saline (drug), two levels of randomization; a balanced subset of Mehta et al. (2011) via Lazic and Essioux (2013). Rendered with a litter intercept; sex is not in the design's model. activity is an integer locomotor activity count.

The page gives the design in one line and fits no model: cell counts per well of six 1536-well plates from a high-throughput screen. Rendered with a plate intercept; row and column are well positions on the plate (coordinates), ignored.

The page describes the nested design and fits no model: six rats randomized to three treatments (two each), each liver cut into three pieces, two measurements per piece; the rats are the experimental units with two levels of subsampling (Sokal and Rohlf 1995). Rats are numbered within treatment and pieces within rat, so the factors are Treatment:Rat and Treatment:Rat:Liver.

The page describes the design and fits no model: ten patients randomized to high or low dietary calcium (five each), blood pressure at three time points (Casella 2008). Rendered with a patient intercept and time as a factor.

The page describes the design and fits no model: 47 rats randomized to drug or saline, distance traveled in the open field per 15-minute interval over 90 minutes. Rendered with a rat intercept and time as a factor.

The page describes the design and its coding and fits no model: weekly engagement of 131 band members over 16 weeks, with TRANS and RECOV provided for a discontinuous growth model around an unexpected football win before the twelfth collection (Bliese and Lang 2016). Rendered as that growth model with a person intercept; the Big Five scores, FEMALE, TENURE and RET.15 are person-level columns not in it.

formula: WBEING ~ HRS + LEAD + G.HRS + LEAD:G.HRS + (1 + LEAD | GRP)
notes: Read the package's tutorial (Bliese 2022, Multilevel Modeling in R 2.7, section 4.1): Final.Model <- lme(WBEING ~ HRS + LEAD + G.HRS + LEAD:G.HRS, random = ~LEAD|GRP), refitted as lmer(WBEING ~ HRS + LEAD*G.HRS + (LEAD|GRP)); the tutorial also fits the null model, random-intercept steps and a glmer of ifelse(WBEING > 3.5, 1, 0). G.HRS, the group mean of HRS, is a column of the table; the other G. and W. columns are group means and group-mean-centered copies (derived), ignored. COHES is not in the model. 7382 soldiers in 99 companies.

Read the package's tutorial (Bliese 2022, group-mean reliability): Null.Model <- lme(HRS ~ 1, random = ~1|GRP, data = bhr2000), the null model for ICC(1) and group-mean reliability; the leadership items and RELIG serve the tutorial's agreement indices and enter no mixed model. 5400 soldiers in 99 companies.

The page names the special issue's three scales but no model, and the package's tutorial uses the table only for rwg(j) agreement. The special issue (Bliese, Halverson and Schriesheim 2002) benchmarks HLM, WABA and random group resampling on whether leadership climate moderates the relation of a stressor to well-being, here task significance and hostility, among 2042 soldiers in 49 companies; rendered with a company intercept. The items LEAD01 to HOSTIL05 make up the scale scores and GLEAD, GTSIG and GHOSTILE are company means (derived), all ignored; SUB is the subject id.

formula: roani ~ time + trans + post + boardindprop + dirageavg + femaledirsprop + debtassets + lnemp + ceotenure + (1 | companyid)
notes: The page describes the panel and its coding and fits no model: 196 firms observed 2007 to 2011 (980 rows; the format says 960), time, trans and post coded for a discontinuous growth model at the 2009 recession, and yearly board-composition predictors, a panel for contrasting fixed-effect and mixed-effect models (Bliese et al. 2020). roani, return on assets, is the one outcome column. Rendered as the growth model plus the predictors with a firm intercept. companyname duplicates companyid and year equals time + 2007, both ignored.

Read the package's tutorial (Bliese 2022, consensus emergence): threelevel <- lme(y ~ time, random = list(group = pdLogChol(~time), person = pdIdent(~1))), group intercepts and time slopes with persons nested in groups, then threelevelCEM adding weights = varExp(form = ~time), the same grouping (Lang and Bliese 2019). person is numbered within group; condition is not in the model. Sherif (1935): eight groups of three, three estimates each.

Read the package's tutorial (Bliese 2022, discontinuous growth models): with TRANS <- ifelse(TIME < 6, 0, 1) and POST <- ifelse(TIME > 5, TIME - 6, 0), tmod <- lme(SCORE ~ TIME + TRANS + POST, random = ~1|ID, tankdat), from Appendix B of Bliese and Lang (2016); TRANS and POST are no columns, so the formula writes them from TIME. CONSC is not in the model. 184 participants, 12 trials of a tank simulation.

Read the package's tutorial (Bliese 2022, section 5.3, growth models): on the job-satisfaction scores stacked by subject, model.6 <- lme(MULTDV ~ TIME*AGE, random = ~TIME|SUBNUM, correlation = corAR1()) and its lmer refit model.6a <- lmer(MULTDV ~ TIME*AGE + (TIME|SUBNUM)); MULTDV is the table's JSAT, and the AR(1) residual correlation is not representable. JOBSAT1 to READY3 are the wide copies of JSAT, COMMIT and READY, and COMMIT and READY are responses the tutorial does not model, all ignored. Bliese and Ployhart (2002), 495 soldiers at three times.

formula: RT ~ shape * color + (1 | ID) + (1 | ID:shape) + (1 | ID:color)
notes: Read the help page example (Hays 1994, table 13.21.2): aov(RT ~ shape*color + Error(ID/(shape*color))), translated to one intercept per error stratum; with one puzzle per participant and cell, the ID:shape:color stratum is the residual. 12 participants, four puzzles each.

Read the help page example: anovaBF(RT ~ shape*color + ID, data = puzzles, whichRandom = 'ID'), Bayes factors over the submodels with ID random; the page names the main-effects model the best. Package default priors (rscaleFixed medium, rscaleRandom nuisance), so documented_prior is blank.
